sense: not casual: of dress, language, manner

terms.gloss: formal (of dress): worn in public, against what one wears at home
evidence: Cic. Fin. 2.77: ut vestītum … aliam domesticam, aliam forēnsem
terms.comment: “Of the forum”, public; of clothes, the dress one goes out in, against domesticus, what one wears at home (Lewis & Short). Suetonius calls formal dress simply forēnsia (Aug. 73). Its other common sense is “of the courts”, forensic.

terms.gloss: formal, serious (of a letter, of speech)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 2.4.1: ūnum familiāre et jocōsum, alterum sevērum et grave
terms.comment: Cicero’s two kinds of letter: the familiar and joking, and the serious and weighty. So informal is familiāris, formal gravis.
Classically “washed”, and so neat, elegant, sumptuous, of a fine dinner or a well-off man (Lewis & Short, s.v. lavō); Morgan–Owens applies it to formal clothes and gives cotīdiānus for informal ones.

phrases.latin: ut vestītum, sīc sententiam habeās aliam domesticam, aliam forēnsem
phrases.english: that you should have one opinion for home and another for public, as you do with your clothes

phrases.latin: reliqua sunt epistulārum genera duo, quae mē magnō opere dēlectant, ūnum familiāre et jocōsum, alterum sevērum et grave
phrases.english: there remain two kinds of letter which give me great pleasure, one familiar and joking, the other serious and formal

phrases.latin: prīmīs tenebrīs vestītū forēnsī ad portam cum duōbus comitibus ignārīs cōnsiliī est ēgressus
phrases.english: as soon as it was dark he went out to the gate, in his ordinary public dress, with two companions who knew nothing of his plan

sources: Lewis & Short: forensis · Lewis & Short: severus · Lewis & Short: lautus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. formal (of clothing); formal: informal (of clothing).
